source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part II: Trend Lines and Channels (introduction)

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; helpers: highest(x,n)/lowest(x,n) over bars 0..n-1, atr(n), swingHigh(k)/swingLow(k) = k-th most recent confirmed pivot, trendLine(...)/channelLine(...) = projected line value at bar 0

candidates.name: TrendLine
candidates.quote: Both trend lines and trend channel lines are straight, diagonal lines that contain the market's price action, but on opposite sides, forming a channel. In a bull trend, the trend line is below the lows and the trend channel line is above the highs.
candidates.description: Foundational primitive: a trend line is the straight line through two confirmed pivot lows (bull) / highs (bear) that contains the price action on its side, projected forward to price the current bar (trendLine[0]).
candidates.pseudocode: p1 = swingLow(2); p2 = swingLow(1); require p2.price > p1.price; slope = (p2.price - p1.price) / (p2.bar - p1.bar); trendLine[0] = p2.price + slope * (0 - p2.bar)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection (not itself the subject of this chapter but a prerequisite) plus line projection from two pivots

notes: Pivot detection itself is mechanized fully in Chapters 13, 14 and 17 mined files; this introduction only defines the two line TYPES (trend line vs. trend channel line).

candidates.name: TrendChannelLine
candidates.quote: Line 4 is a trend channel line in a bull trend and is above the highs, and line 9 is a trend channel line in a bear trend and is below the lows.
candidates.description: Primitive: the trend channel line is a parallel of the trend line anchored at the pivot on the opposite side that lies between the trend line's two anchors. channelLine[0] is its value at bar 0.
candidates.pseudocode: anchor = swing high between swingLow(2).bar and swingLow(1).bar; channelLine[0] = anchor.price + slope * (0 - anchor.bar)

complexity.reason: needs the trend line plus a search for the extreme pivot between its anchors

candidates.name: HorizontalSupportResistanceLine
candidates.quote: Lines 5 and 6 are horizontal lines in a trading range, which is just a horizontal channel. Line 5 is above the highs and is a resistance line and line 6 is below the lows and is a support line.
candidates.description: Special case of TP2-01/02 with zero slope: resistance = highest high over the range window, support = lowest low over the same window.
candidates.pseudocode: resistance = highest(high, rangeBars); support = lowest(low, rangeBars)

complexity.reason: plain window highest/lowest; no pivot projection is needed once slope is zero

candidates.name: ChannelShapeClassification
candidates.quote: The lines defining the channel most often are parallel or roughly parallel, but are convergent in wedges and most other triangles, and divergent in expanding triangles.
candidates.description: Classify the channel by comparing its width (channel line minus trend line) now versus k bars ago: narrowing width flags a wedge/triangle context (favors a reversal read), widening flags an expanding triangle (favors a range read), and roughly equal width is a standard parallel channel (favors continuation).
candidates.pseudocode: widthNow = channelLine[0] - trendLine[0]; widthEarlier = channelLine[k] - trendLine[k]; isWedge = widthNow < widthEarlier * convergeFraction; isExpanding = widthNow > widthEarlier / convergeFraction

complexity.reason: needs both projected lines evaluated at two points in time

notes: Chapter 14 mechanizes the wedge case in more detail (T14-08).

candidates.name: OpeningRangeBreakoutBothSides
candidates.quote: Traders would buy on a stop at one tick above the high and go short at one tick below the low of the opening range.
candidates.description: Intraday: after the first orBars bars of the session (the opening range), buy on a close above its high / sell on a close below its low, entering at the next open.
candidates.pseudocode: orHigh = highest(high, orBars) over the session's first orBars bars; close[0] > orHigh
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the opening range high / sell stop below its low (mechanized: next bar open)

complexity.reason: a session-anchored highest/lowest window plus a breakout test

candidates.name: ExpandingTriangleHeightTarget
candidates.quote: The market broke to the upside and a minimal target was a measured move up equal to the height of the expanding triangle.
candidates.description: Profit target after a range/triangle breakout: exit when price has travelled the height of the pattern (captured at the breakout) beyond the breakout level.
candidates.pseudocode: target = breakoutLevel + heightMultiple * (rangeHigh - rangeLow); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the measured move target

complexity.reason: the pattern height and breakout level must be captured at entry and held as state; no pivot projection is needed for the horizontal-range special case

rejected.quote: with so many institutions now shorting as much as they are buying, a resistance line is just as likely to be where they are initiating a new short as it is that they are exiting or distributing their longs.
Curved lines and bands are too subjective and therefore require too much thought when you are trying to place trades quickly.
rejected.reason: explicit rejection of a technique by Brooks himself; no test given, either to accept or reject curved lines mechanically.

rejected.quote: Since the final six bars of yesterday were bull trend bars, only a second-entry short could be considered, but there was no reasonable signal.
rejected.reason: restates the existing consecutive-trend-bar countertrend filter (Chapter 10's ConsecutiveTrendBarsBlockCountertrend); no new test.

chapter_summary: Part II's introduction defines the vocabulary the rest of the part mechanizes: trend lines (support/resistance drawn through swing pivots), trend channel lines (the parallel line on the opposite side), horizontal lines as the zero-slope special case, and a slope-based classification of channel/wedge/expanding-triangle shape. It also produced two concrete, more mechanizable ideas from its single worked figure: an opening-range breakout taken in both directions, and a measured-move target from a range's height. All the line primitives here are deliberately high-level; Chapters 13, 14 and 17 mined separately give the detailed touch/break/overshoot entries and exits built on top of them.
